title: Wedgwood Makes Queen's Ware
text:
In the 1760s Josiah Wedgwood was a successful potter in Staffordshire, making a refined cream-colored earthenware. In 1765 he received an order for a tea service from Queen Charlotte, wife of George III. He executed it with great care and then asked permission to call his cream ware Queen's Ware and to style himself Potter to Her Majesty. Both were granted.

Wedgwood understood what this meant. In his letters to his business partner Thomas Bentley, he wrote repeatedly about how fashion flowed downward: if the court and the great families adopted his wares, the middle classes would want them too. He sought aristocratic patrons, gave them special designs, and advertised the connections.

He also changed how pottery was sold. He opened showrooms in London where fashionable customers could see whole table services elegantly displayed, and he rearranged the displays regularly to keep people coming back. He produced catalogues, offered sets in many patterns, guaranteed replacement of goods broken in transit, and in some cases offered money back to dissatisfied customers. When he made a huge service for Catherine the Great of Russia in the early 1770s, decorated with views of British scenes, he first displayed it in London, drawing crowds.

Queen's Ware became the standard tableware of middle-class Britain and was exported across Europe and America. Wedgwood became one of the richest manufacturers of his age.
lesson: Endorsement from people others admire can turn a product into an aspiration. How something is shown and sold can matter as much as how it is made.
people: Josiah Wedgwood, Thomas Bentley, Queen Charlotte
source: Josiah Wedgwood's letters to Thomas Bentley; Neil McKendrick, Josiah Wedgwood: An Eighteenth-Century Entrepreneur in Salesmanship and Marketing Techniques, Economic History Review (1960); Brian Dolan, Josiah Wedgwood (2004)
